**Case Vignette: "Marcus"**

Marcus is a 53-year-old man of Oceania descent, a senior captain for a major international airline. He is married, with three adult children. He presents for therapy at his wife’s urging, though he is visibly uncomfortable in the clinical setting. He sits forward in his chair, hands clasped, eyes scanning the room as if checking for exits. His voice is low, controlled, but occasionally cracks when he speaks of the past.

The story begins eighteen months ago, during a layover in a politically unstable region. Marcus and his co-pilot were taken from their hotel at gunpoint by a paramilitary group. For three days, they were held in a concrete room. Marcus was blindfolded, beaten, and subjected to mock executions. His captors demanded information about airline security protocols, but he had none to give. They did not believe him. The torture was systematic: sleep deprivation, stress positions, and the constant, visceral threat of death. He heard his co-pilot being tortured in the next room. On the third day, a ransom was paid, and they were released.

Since then, Marcus has not been the same. He returned to flying after six weeks of administrative leave, but the cockpit now feels like a cage. The moment the cabin door closes, his heart rate spikes. He feels a pressure on his chest, as if the seatbelt is too tight. He has developed a hypervigilance that he cannot switch off. During pre-flight checks, he finds himself staring at the emergency exits for too long, mentally rehearsing escape routes that have nothing to do with the aircraft. His first officer, a younger man, has noticed that Marcus now insists on flying with the cockpit door locked at all times, even on the ground, which is against standard procedure for boarding. When asked about it, Marcus becomes curt and dismissive.

At home, he is irritable and withdrawn. He avoids intimacy with his wife, not because he does not love her, but because he cannot tolerate the vulnerability. He has nightmares almost every night, but he refuses to describe them to her. He says only that he wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced he is back in that room. He has started drinking—a glass of whiskey before bed to "take the edge off," then two, then three. His wife found him in the garage at 2 AM last week, sitting in his car with the engine off, staring at the dashboard. He told her he was "just checking something."

Marcus has also developed a profound distrust of authority. He feels that his airline did not do enough to protect him, and he now sees every company policy as a potential trap. He has become obsessed with security protocols, often second-guessing his dispatchers and ground crew. He knows this is irrational, but he cannot stop. His PCL-5 score of 70 reflects severe, pervasive symptoms: intrusive memories that strike mid-flight, avoidance of any news about the region where he was held, negative beliefs about the world being dangerous, and a constant state of hyperarousal that leaves him exhausted.

He tells me that the worst part is not the memory of the pain, but the silence. In the cockpit, at 35,000 feet, when the radio goes quiet, he hears the sound of that concrete room. He hears his own breathing, his own heart, and the distant, muffled cries of his co-pilot. He knows he is safe. He knows the numbers on the instruments are correct. But his body does not believe him. He is a pilot who no longer trusts the sky.
